content.title: Walkthroughs: a cited, validated story of a code change stack
content.intent: This stack adds Walkthroughs, a generated story of a code change or stack with cited code as evidence, so reviewers can follow agent-written work without reading every line.

chapters.label: Why Walkthroughs
chapters.caption: Reviewing agent-written stacks is the bottleneck, so this stack generates a guided story with code as evidence.
chapters.body: Coding agents produce more code than people can review, and walls of text make it worse [1]. A Walkthrough is a short story about a code change or a stack, where cited code is the evidence [2]. Five layers build it: the format and its validator (#3087), provider reads through plugins (#3088), stored versions (#3090), the generation Turn and its submit tool (#3124), and the API behind the `walkthroughs` experiment (#3133). The review risk is in who can read what, and in how a version row recovers from a dead run.
asks: Who can start a Walkthrough today?
What happens when two people click at once?

chapters.label: The cited format
chapters.caption: The model writes a cited outline with fixed slots per change type, and Junior adds everything else.
chapters.body: The model fills a fixed set of slots for each change type, such as cause and fix for a bug fix [1]. That follows the earlier research on review, which suggested the model fill a template instead of inventing structure [3]. Each chapter cites code by PR, path, and line range, and never copies code or message text [2]. Junior adds the layers, excerpts, message text, and skip counts to make the stored document. A later slice already loosens these slots [4].

decisions.claim: Fixed slots per change type are the right first contract for a Walkthrough.
decisions.concern: The story-first slice (#3164) drops per-chapter types, slots, and splits, so this format changes right after it lands.

asks: Why is the document schema versioned already?

chapters.label: The validator gate
chapters.caption: Every citation must resolve against the real diff, and every hunk that is not mechanical must be cited or excused.
chapters.body: Mechanical files, such as lockfiles, generated paths, pure renames, and whitespace-only edits, are dropped before the model sees them, and only counts remain [1]. A code citation must land inside a diff hunk or, on the head side, inside a file read at the head commit [2]. Each hunk must overlap a citation, or its file must be listed as not covered [3]. Excerpts are then copied from the provider diff, never from the model [4].

decisions.claim: Whitespace-only edits are mechanical, so hiding them from the model and from coverage is safe.
decisions.concern: In Python or YAML, indentation changes behavior, and such a hunk would show only as a skipped count.

asks: Can a hand-edited file under dist/ be cited?

chapters.label: Reading code through plugins
chapters.caption: Core asks the provider's plugin for the stack, the diff, and files, using Junior's system identity.
chapters.body: Core never calls a provider API. A plugin implements three read hooks: the stack, the diff between two commits, and one file at a commit [1]. Core runs them as a system actor with an auth handler that does nothing, so a read never uses a person's credentials or asks anyone to authorize [2]. The GitHub plugin asks the Stacks API first, falls back to walking base branches, and keeps only open layers plus the requested one [3]. The diff compares exact SHAs, so a push during generation cannot change what is described [4].
asks: What happens when the base-branch walk finds two children?

chapters.label: One version per snapshot
chapters.caption: A new table keeps one live version per stack at its commits, so a repeat click joins instead of generating again.
chapters.body: The migration adds one table and its indexes, so it is safe to run on existing data [1]. A version is keyed by a hash of each layer's number and SHAs, and a partial unique index allows one non-failed row per key. A second click hits that conflict and joins the running or ready version, and a failed row does not block a retry [2]. Every Conversation list now hides generation Conversations with a subquery on this table [3], so a rollback must revert that filter along with the table.

decisions.claim: The subquery added to every Conversation list stays cheap because the unique index serves it.
decisions.concern: Lists are a hot path, and no query plan or timing backs this.

asks: Why is there no foreign key to the generation Conversation?

chapters.label: The generation Turn
chapters.caption: A generation Turn gets submitWalkthrough and loses every tool that reaches people or other agents.
chapters.body: A run that carries a version gets its own Turn behavior: no agents, review desk, subscriptions, or user customization, and the submit tool turned on [1]. The tool re-reads the diff, the cited head files, and the cited messages, runs the validator, and sends problems back to the model as a tool input error. Only a clean submission stores the document and marks the row ready [2]. Head-side citations may come from at most 30 files [3]. In a real 5-PR stack run, that cap cost a rejection round [4].

decisions.claim: Thirty cited head files per submission is enough for a stack.
decisions.concern: The cap throws instead of trimming, so a large stack pays a full rejection round to get under it.

asks: Does a rejected submission cost a new diff read?

chapters.label: Starting a Walkthrough
chapters.caption: A dashboard POST reads the stack, claims a version, and enqueues a hidden public Conversation that runs the skill.
chapters.body: The routes return 404 unless the `walkthroughs` experiment is on [1]. A POST reads the stack, looks for the source Conversation in the footer marker that Junior writes in its PR bodies, and keeps it only when it is public [2]. It then claims the version. Only the request that started it enqueues a public Conversation whose first message runs the skill, and a failed enqueue fails the version [3]. Both routes check the source Conversation again on read, because the document quotes it [4].

decisions.claim: Finding the source Conversation from the PR footer marker is good enough for this stack.
decisions.concern: The reviewer asked for the stored code change to Conversation mapping instead, and #3174 replaces this lookup above the stack.

decisions.claim: Any signed-in viewer may start and read a Walkthrough of any repository the GitHub App can read.
decisions.concern: Reads use Junior's system identity and the routes check only the source Conversation, so private code can reach viewers without repo access.

asks: Is the generation Conversation readable by its id?

chapters.label: Failure and retry
chapters.caption: A Turn that ends without a stored Walkthrough fails its version, and a stale generating row times out on the next click.
chapters.body: The Turn worker looks up the version for its Conversation and passes it into the run [1]. When the run completes, the worker fails the version if it is still generating, which covers a model that stops without a clean submission [2]. A run that throws skips that step. Unless the worker retries the Turn, the row stays generating until a click on the same snapshot, 30 minutes later, fails it [3].

decisions.claim: A crashed generation may keep its snapshot in generating until a click after 30 minutes.
decisions.concern: Nothing sweeps stale rows, so every viewer sees generating until someone clicks again after the timeout.

asks: What happens to a slow run that a timeout already failed?

chapters.label: How we know it works
chapters.caption: Unit and integration tests cover GitHub reads, the submit tool, and the API flow from start to retry.
chapters.body: Unit tests reject unresolved citations, uncovered hunks, and a cause chapter that cites only prose. The GitHub tests walk a base-branch chain that forks [1]. An integration test runs the submit tool: a bad citation leaves the row generating, and a good one stores a document with excerpts, messages, and skip counts [2]. The API test checks the experiment gate, one Turn per snapshot, hidden lists, and a fresh retry after a Turn ends with no Walkthrough [3].
asks: Does any test run a real model generation?

chapters.label: What to watch after shipping
chapters.caption: Failed and stuck version rows, and generation cost, show whether generations work in practice.
chapters.body: Watch `junior_walkthrough_versions`. Rows failed with "The Turn ended without a Walkthrough." mean the model gave up or never passed validation [1]. "Generation timed out." failures, or rows generating for over 30 minutes, mean runs are crashing. Cost per generation comes from the generation Conversation's `cost_usd` metrics [2]. Runs near $5 or 80 tool calls are hitting the generation Turn limits [3].
